Search Result Suppression: How to Push Negative Results Off Google's First Page

By RMA — Web Reputation Agency

Search result suppression means making other, accurate and relevant pages outrank the negative ones, so that a damaging article or post drops from page one to page two or lower, where very few people ever look. It does not delete anything: it changes what people see first when they search your name or brand. Done properly, it relies on genuine assets you own or earn, and in Italy it typically takes several months to show stable results.

What suppression actually changes in Google

Search result suppression changes the ranking order for specific queries, not the existence of the negative page. When someone in Milan types your company name, Google shows roughly ten organic results plus features such as a knowledge panel, images, news and "People also ask". Every one of those slots is limited, so each strong, relevant page you add competes for the same space as the unwanted result.

This is why the technique works best on branded and name searches. For a query like "Rossi Costruzioni Roma", Google wants to show the official site, the company's profiles and reliable coverage about it. If those pages are well built and clearly connected to the entity, they naturally rise, and a hostile blog post with weak authority tends to sink. The approach differs from removal and deindexing, which act on the URL itself; we explain those differences in our article on removal, deindexing and ranking suppression.

Mapping page one before building anything

The first step is a precise map of today's results for every query that matters, because you can only push down negative search results you have measured. We check the main brand name, the name plus city, the name plus words like "opinioni", "truffa" or "recensioni", and the names of founders or directors. Results are captured in an Italian-language session located in Italy, with Google.it, since a page that ranks fifth in Rome may rank differently for an English search from London.

For each position we record the URL, owner, authority, freshness and sentiment. The output tells us three things:

  • which slots are already held by positive or neutral pages you control;
  • which slots are held by third parties that could be strengthened as allies (a trade association profile, a fair interview);
  • which negative results are weak enough to be overtaken, and which are strong news domains that will take longer.

This map also reveals gaps: missing social profiles, an "about" page that never mentions the full company name, or a site that Google cannot crawl properly. Fixing those gaps is often the cheapest gain in the whole project.

Owned and earned assets that can outrank a negative page

The assets that work are the ones Google already trusts for entity queries: your own domain, verified profiles, and independent sites that write about you. Each must be genuinely useful and clearly about the same person or company, otherwise it will not hold its position.

Owned assets

Your website is the anchor. Pages such as "Chi siamo", leadership bios, press area and case studies can each rank separately if they are distinct, indexed and internally linked. A second property, for example a project blog on a subdomain or a separate site for a foundation, can occupy another slot when it has real content rather than thin copies. Profiles on LinkedIn, YouTube, Instagram, Crunchbase-style directories and the Google Business Profile complete the owned layer.

Earned assets

Interviews in sector magazines, speaker pages at conferences, chamber of commerce listings, university or association pages and podcast appearances carry independent authority. For an Italian manufacturer, a feature in a regional business newspaper or a trade fair exhibitor profile in Bologna or Milan often outranks a complaint thread far more easily than another self-published page.

Suppression succeeds when every new page would deserve to rank even if there were no negative result to push down. Assets built only as filler rarely hold their position.

Technical signals that help each asset

Consistent naming, Organization or Person schema on the main site, links from the site to every official profile and back, and descriptive titles that include the exact brand name all help Google connect the assets to one entity. That entity clarity also feeds AI-generated answers, a topic we cover in how generative search is changing reputation work.

How long it takes to suppress negative Google results

For most Italian businesses and professionals, visible movement appears in two to four months, and a stable page one usually needs six months or more. The timeline depends on the strength of the negative page, the competition for the query and how much legitimate material exists about you.

Type of negative resultTypical difficultyRealistic expectation
Anonymous blog or small forum threadLowOften moves off page one within a few months
Review platform or complaint site pageMediumRequires several strong profiles and earned coverage
Article on a national news outletHighCan take many months; may only drop a few positions
Result for a generic, non-branded queryVery highUsually not a realistic suppression target

Google updates, a fresh wave of coverage or a new complaint can reverse progress, so the work is measured monthly against the original map rather than declared finished after one good week.

What cannot be suppressed, and when to choose another route

Some results resist suppression: very recent news with high public interest, official sources such as court or government sites, and content that keeps being shared and linked. When a story is still developing, new pages simply cannot gather authority fast enough.

In those cases suppression should be combined with, or replaced by, other tools. Unlawful content, such as defamation under art. 595 of the Italian Criminal Code or personal data that should no longer be processed, may qualify for removal or for deindexing under GDPR art. 17 and the Google Spain ruling (C-131/12). Negative autocomplete suggestions need their own procedure, described in our guide to removing negative Google suggestions. Suppression is then the layer that protects page one while those requests are processed.

Black-hat shortcuts, such as networks of fake sites, bought links or fabricated reviews, violate Google's spam policies. They tend to collapse after core or spam updates and can drag the brand's own site down with them, which is why a serious agency does not use them and cannot honestly guarantee a fixed final position.

A practical suppression plan for an Italian company

The work follows a fixed sequence so that effort goes where it changes rankings. A typical plan for a business with one damaging result in fourth position looks like this:

  1. Audit page one and the neighbouring results on page two for each branded query.
  2. Fix the main website: crawlability, distinct pages for team, history and press, schema markup.
  3. Complete and verify the key profiles, linking them to the site.
  4. Plan two or three pieces of earned coverage per quarter with trade media or associations.
  5. Publish regularly on owned channels so that fresh, relevant pages keep appearing.
  6. Track positions monthly and adjust where an asset stalls.

Ownership matters as much as tactics. Someone inside the company must approve content, provide real material (projects, data, photos) and avoid actions that create new negative coverage.
